headline: Joint U.S.–South Korean military exercises began on August 17 and will run through August 27. The drills will include joint operations aimed at improving the allies’ combat readiness. South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff spokesman Jang Do-young said the allies will jointly “assess the country’s military capabilities” during the exercises. However, on Sunday evening, the U.S. president said he was “not happy” with US participation “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un”. He added that they were costly and “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a country that, as long as Donald J Trump has been president, has been unthreatening and respectful”. Trump added that it was too late to cancel the drills so he had ordered the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, to “substantially reduce” them. He also said South Korea had refused to help in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic republic of Iran”. On August 14, KCNA published a statement from a North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson, who described the upcoming Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises as “aggressive.”

headline: The Ukrainian Armed Forces have been using British-made long-range drones to conduct deep strikes inside Russian territory for the past six months, according to The Times. The attacks have involved the jet-powered Nyan One Way Effector (OWE) loitering munition, developed by Callen-Lenz, a FalconWorks division of defense contractor BAE Systems, as well as another classified British model with a stated range of more than 965 km (600 miles). British-made drones have been used to strike oil refineries and logistics facilities in Moscow, Yaroslavl, including the Slavneft-YANOS refinery, and Volgograd Oblasts. Nyan UAVs have also reportedly been used against targets in Belgorod Oblast. Although Ukrainian-built systems still make up the bulk of Ukraine’s long-range drone fleet, the integration of British-manufactured systems would mark a direct shift by London toward supplying ready-made strike weapons for attacks deep inside Russia.

headline: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called for direct talks with North Korea to formally end the Korean War, seeking to replace the 73-year-old armistice with a permanent peace agreement. The Korean War never formally ended with a peace treaty; instead, an armistice was signed in July 1953, meaning the Korean Peninsula has technically remained in a state of war ever since. From my understanding, North Korea previously pursued unification with the South. However, after Kim Jong Un abandoned that policy and began treating South Korea as a separate, hostile state, it seems that the options for a peaceful settlement have become much more limited. A permanent peace agreement could also be difficult for Pyongyang to accept, as it could imply recognition of South Korea as a legitimate, separate state.

headline: More than 1,300 Strava users have publicly logged workouts from U.S. military sites across the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area, according to an investigation by Sky News cited by Task & Purpose. The exposure is particularly concerning because many of these installations have subsequently been targeted by Iran. At Muwaffaq Al Salti Air Base in Jordan, for example, personnel regularly posted runs around the installation. Activity resumed in April and later became concentrated around barracks; the housing area was struck in July, killing three U.S. soldiers. The issue isn't new. In 2018, Strava's public heat maps exposed previously undisclosed military locations and details about base layouts. The Pentagon subsequently prohibited personnel from using geolocation features on personal or government devices. CENTCOM has since issued additional OPSEC guidance, including restrictions implemented when Operation Epic Fury began. Yet publicly available Strava data shows personnel are still exposing their locations. This is particularly notable given Adm. Brad Cooper's warning last month that Iran was using troops' photos, videos and other cellphone-generated information to assess strike effectiveness and help target U.S. personnel. Below are screenshots taken from the Strava app today showing activity at Muwaffaq Al Salti Air Base, Jordan and Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia. The blue lines are tracks uploaded to the app by users with the darker color representing higher usage of route.

headline: The future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN-79) has successfully completed Navy acceptance trials, marking a major milestone toward delivery of the second Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier to the fleet, as announced by the U.S. Navy's Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE). Acceptance trials are the Navy's formal evaluation of the completed ship to determine whether it meets its required performance and capabilities. With the trials complete, Kennedy moves toward delivery to the Navy in March 2027, followed by additional post-delivery work, crew training and certification before entering operational service. Kennedy is the second ship of the Ford class, incorporating systems including EMALS electromagnetic catapults, Advanced Arresting Gear and Advanced Weapons Elevators.

headline: Five people were injured in a shooting involving multiple shooters near a residence hall at Virginia State University (VSU) early Saturday. Police responding around 1:30 a.m. found five people with gunshot wounds. One victim is in critical condition; four others suffered nonlife-threatening injuries. Only one victim has been confirmed as a VSU student, with investigators believing the others may be from the surrounding community. Authorities say the shooting was not a drive-by and are searching for multiple suspects. No arrests have been reported. The campus was temporarily locked down, with a significant law-enforcement presence remaining as the investigation continues. The shooting comes just days before classes are scheduled to begin Monday.

headline: STATEMENT FROM COMMANDER OF U.S. CENTRAL COMMAND “My time aboard USS Abraham Lincoln yesterday was awe-inspiring. I wish every American could see the crew in action. You would beam with absolute pride when witnessing their camaraderie, teamwork and resilience. Here’s an important fact: Of the U.S. Navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, the Lincoln currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health. This doesn’t mean that all is perfect. Find any of the nearly 4 million Navy veterans in America today and they will likely tell you that service at sea for long periods isn’t for everyone. It is uniquely challenging and tough, and every single one of us, including me, reacts to stressors in different ways. I’ve long believed that mental health is another aspect of individual health and requires our attention just like physical health and spiritual health. I applaud Lincoln’s leadership — the senior enlisted leaders in the Chief Petty Officers Mess in particular — for stepping up and making mental health and crew resilience a leadership priority. To all our Sailors and Marines aboard the ship, keep up the great work and fair winds and following seas on the journey home.” Adm. Brad Cooper, CENTCOM Commander
